newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Rebel politician draws crowds to Singapore rallies.
newsitem.headline: Rebel politician draws crowds to Singapore rallies.

text.p: The government calls him a "proven liar", the Straits Times newspaper says he is "guilty of deceit", but the head of Singapore's main opposition party is drawing large crowds to his daily election rallies.

Chee Soon Juan, the leader of the Singapore Democratic Party (SDP), is taking full advantage of the attacks on him in the state-run media to try to convince Singaporeans to elect opposition members of parliament (MPs), his supporters say.
"For the opposition, these rallies are the only time they can speak directly to the people," civil servant Edward Lim, 43, told Reuters at one of Chee's outdoor rallies on Sunday evening.
"Many of the people here are supporters, of course, but most just want to hear him for themselves. They don't get a chance anywhere else," Lim said.
Chee and the leaders of the other small Singapore opposition parties face an uphill struggle in the general election on January 2.

The governing People's Action Party (PAP), which has ruled Singapore since it became self-governing in 1959, is already assured of a majority in the 83-seat parliament because it faces challenges in only 36 seats.
But Chee hopes the fact that the PAP is already back in power will encourage voters in the contested seats to support parties able to provide alternative voices in parliament.

They praise the economic successes of the PAP, which has transformed Singapore from colonial trading post to one of the richest countries in Asia, but they oppose what they say are the authoritarian methods the PAP has used to achieve it.
Chee says the Singapore newspapers and television have never given him a fair hearing.
"I have been interviewed by the BBC, CNN, Hong Kong television, many broadcasters...but not by TCS (state Television Corp of Singapore)," Chee told his audience on Sunday.
PAP supporters say Chee has always had a fair hearing and say he admitted in court during a libel case that he had lied.
The Straits Times, which closely reflects PAP thinking, also bases its attacks on Chee on legal cases which he has lost over the last few years.
But many voters attending Chee's rallies appeared to have open minds. Several said he may have been treated unfairly in the daily barrage of attacks from the PAP.
Chee has had other troubles, too. He was fired from his job as a lecturer, accused of misusing university funds. He lost a libel suit brought by his former boss, a PAP parliamentarian.

Chee had to sell his house to pay the Singapore $450,000 (US$321,000) in costs and damages from one legal case and was recently one of a group of 12 people fined a total of S$120,000 after being sued for defamation by an opposition MP.

"I've come because I am curious," David Siow, an engineer attending one of Chee's rallies on Friday evening, told Reuters. "We hear about him every day in the newspapers, but it is always negative and you never know if what they say about him is true."
Penelope Wong, a 33-year-old civil servant, said she thought some voters might support Chee because of the attacks on him.
"Even if they think the criticism of him is true, many people sympathise with Chee. They think he is being persecuted," Wong said on Sunday evening.
SDP workers say the large crowds at Chee's rallies -- police estimated 8,000 listened to his speech on Sunday -- probably did not reflect his likely support at the election.

"I think Chee has a 50:50 chance of winning in the seat he is contesting," said one party worker, who declined to be identified. "Some of these people can't vote or have come from outside the area...But at least they are listening."
